title: How Tiny Finland Held Off the Soviet Union in 1939
hook: In January 1940, Finnish skiers slid out of a forest and found a Soviet column miles long, frozen in the snow.
thumbnail_picture: Big close-up on the right of an abandoned Soviet tank half buried in deep snow on a narrow forest road, icicles on its gun, with a Finnish ski soldier in a white cape and wool cap on skis staring at it wide-eyed in shock, dark frosty pine forest behind, cold blue dusk light, left third of the frame empty snow.
description:
How did tiny Finland hold off the Soviet Union in the Winter War of 1939-1940? Follow the ski patrols, the frozen forests and the Mannerheim Line to find out how a small country survived a giant army.

The story of the Winter War, which began on 30 November 1939: why the border near Leningrad mattered, how Finnish skiers cut a Soviet column into pieces, and how Finland lost land but kept its independence.

Sources and further reading:
- William R. Trotter, "A Frozen Hell: The Russo-Finnish Winter War of 1939-1940" (1991)
- Vesa Nenye, Peter Munter, Toni Wirtanen and Chris Birks, "Finland at War: The Winter War 1939-40" (Osprey, 2015)
- Allan Chew, "The White Death: The Epic of the Soviet-Finnish Winter War" (1971)
- Finnish National Archives and Finnish Defence Forces historical publications on the Winter War
tags: how finland beat the soviet union

scenes.narration: In January 1940, Finnish skiers slid out of a forest and found a Soviet column miles long, frozen in the snow.
scenes.caption: RAATE ROAD, 1940
scenes.picture: A Finnish ski soldier in a long white cape, white hood and grey wool cap stands at the edge of a dark pine forest, staring down a narrow snowy road packed with a silent, frozen column of Soviet trucks and tanks stretching far away, pale winter light.

scenes.narration: Tanks, trucks, field guns, all silent. Thousands of men never reached the end of that road.
scenes.caption: A SILENT COLUMN
scenes.picture: Close view of an abandoned dark green Soviet tank half buried in snow on a forest road, frost and long icicles hanging from its gun barrel, a toppled army truck beside it, no people, grey cold morning.

scenes.narration: Finland had about forty-five times fewer people, its troops were outnumbered roughly three to one, and it was far worse off in tanks and planes. <short pause> How did it hold on?
scenes.caption: 45x SMALLER
scenes.picture: Three small Finnish soldiers in long white capes stand on a snowy hill looking down at a vast dark mass of marching Soviet soldiers filling the whole valley below, tiny group against a huge army, grey winter sky.

scenes.narration: People give three explanations. One is mostly a myth, and it's the most famous of them all.
scenes.caption: THREE THEORIES
scenes.picture: Three plain objects lie on a rough wooden table in a dim log hut lit by one oil lamp: a chunk of grey granite, a frosted glass jar of ice, and a rifle with a white-painted barrel. No people, warm lamp glow.

scenes.narration: To see why, go back to Leningrad, the Soviet Union's second city, home to about three million people.
scenes.caption: LENINGRAD, 1939
scenes.picture: Wide view of Leningrad in autumn 1939: a broad river lined with tall pastel palaces, a golden needle-shaped spire, and a few people in long coats walking along the stone embankment under a grey evening sky.

scenes.narration: The Finnish border sat just thirty-two kilometres away, close enough, planners feared, for enemy guns to reach the city.
scenes.caption: 32 KM AWAY
scenes.picture: A long old field cannon on a wooden-wheeled carriage sits on a flat plain of bare autumn birch and pine trees, its barrel pointing toward a faint city skyline on the far hazy horizon, cold light, no people.

scenes.narration: So in autumn 1939, Moscow asked Finland to pull its border back on the Karelian Isthmus and give up some land.
scenes.caption: THE DEMAND
scenes.picture: Two men in dark 1939 overcoats sit across a long polished table in a stately room with tall windows. One man slides a closed folder toward the other, who frowns with his arms crossed, pale winter light.

scenes.narration: Moscow offered more remote forest, and wanted islands and Hanko. Finland refused: homes, farms and defences lay there, and Moscow might keep asking.
scenes.caption: FINLAND SAYS NO
scenes.picture: A Finnish farmer in a wool cap and heavy brown coat stands at the gate of his wooden farmhouse beside a red-painted barn and a ploughed field, worried but firm face, arms folded, autumn dusk.

scenes.narration: Look at the numbers. Finland had under four million people. The Soviet Union had roughly one hundred and seventy million.
scenes.delivery: slow, letting the gap sink in
scenes.caption: 3.7 vs 170 MILLION
scenes.picture: A tiny village of a few red wooden cottages beside a frozen lake sits at the bottom of the picture, while behind it a gigantic dark blurred crowd of people fills the whole horizon, grey winter sky.

scenes.narration: On 30 November 1939, bombs fell on Helsinki, and hundreds of thousands of Soviet soldiers crossed the frozen border.
scenes.caption: 30 NOVEMBER 1939
scenes.picture: Smoke rises over the rooftops of Helsinki in 1939, old stone buildings and a pale church tower below, two frightened people in winter coats look up at distant aircraft in a cold pale sky.

scenes.narration: Finland's army was brave, but badly short of tanks, anti-tank guns and proper uniforms.
scenes.caption: SHORT OF EVERYTHING
scenes.picture: A line of Finnish reservists in mismatched civilian winter coats and fur caps carrying old rifles trudge along a snowy forest track, tired worried faces, one man with a scarf wrapped around his face.

scenes.narration: Its commander, Marshal Mannerheim, was seventy-two, and he knew exactly how little he had to work with.
scenes.caption: MARSHAL MANNERHEIM
scenes.picture: An elderly tall Finnish general with white hair, stern lined face and a long grey military greatcoat stands at a wooden window looking out at falling snow, weary expression, lamp glow in a plain wooden room.

scenes.narration: So here's the first theory: the Finns hid behind a mighty fortress called the Mannerheim Line.
scenes.caption: THEORY ONE
scenes.picture: A Finnish ski soldier in a long white cape, white hood and grey wool cap peers out from a log-covered bunker mouth in a snowy pine forest toward a misty open field, determined face, soft falling snow.

scenes.narration: Newspapers abroad pictured an enormous wall of steel and concrete, running across the whole Karelian Isthmus.
scenes.caption: THE LEGEND
scenes.picture: A gigantic imagined grey concrete fortress wall with huge gun turrets stretches across a snowy plain to the horizon, exaggerated and heroic, painted in a bold storybook style, dramatic sky, no people.

scenes.narration: But go and look, and you find mostly trenches, log bunkers, and rows of granite boulders meant to stop tanks.
scenes.caption: THE REALITY
scenes.picture: Rows of large rough grey granite boulders set in lines in a snowy forest clearing, with a muddy zigzag trench and a log-roofed bunker behind them, no people, cold grey light.

scenes.narration: There were only a couple of hundred concrete bunkers, most of them small, spread along more than a hundred kilometres.
scenes.caption: FEW BUNKERS
scenes.picture: A single small grey concrete bunker half hidden under snow among pine trees, with a long empty line of snowy forest stretching far into the distance on both sides, quiet and lonely.

scenes.narration: Still, it held over two months, and tanks did get stuck among those boulders. It mattered, but it wasn't everything.
scenes.caption: HELPFUL, NOT ENOUGH
scenes.picture: A dark green Soviet tank tilted and stuck against a wall of granite boulders on a snowy field, smoke rising from its engine, while a Finnish ski soldier in a long white cape watches from a trench in the foreground.

scenes.narration: Second theory: the cold. It was one of the coldest winters in memory, with nights dropping to about minus forty.
scenes.caption: THEORY TWO: -40°C
scenes.picture: A frosted birch tree trunk in a still forest before dawn, thick white frost on the bark and branches, a thin cloud of cold mist hanging in the air, deep blue light, no people.

scenes.narration: Finns were used to it. Thin-coated Soviets weren't, and frost took thousands. But cold alone can't explain the road battles.
scenes.caption: HIT HARDER
scenes.picture: A shivering Soviet soldier in a thin brown greatcoat with frost on his eyebrows stands beside a Finnish soldier in a thick white cape and fur-lined hood, both in deep snow in a forest, breath steaming.

scenes.narration: So the cold can't be the whole answer. The real difference was how each side moved through the forest.
scenes.caption: A NEW CLUE
scenes.picture: A thick snowy pine forest seen from high above, a narrow road cutting through the trees and faint ski tracks weaving between the trunks beside it, pale winter daylight, no people.

scenes.narration: Soviet columns stuck to the roads, because tanks, trucks and heavy guns can't cross a forest. And those roads were narrow.
scenes.caption: TIED TO ROADS
scenes.picture: A long line of dark green tanks and horse-drawn carts crawls along a single narrow snowy road squeezed between walls of dark pine trees, cramped and slow, grey sky.

scenes.narration: Finnish soldiers had grown up in those woods. Many had been on skis since before they could read.
scenes.caption: BORN ON SKIS
scenes.picture: A small Finnish boy in a wool hat and mittens glides on wooden skis between birch trees beside a frozen lake, his father in a plain coat chopping wood in the background, golden low winter sun.

scenes.narration: They pulled on white capes and slid between the trees without a sound.
scenes.caption: WHITE CAPES
scenes.picture: Three Finnish ski soldiers in long white capes and white hoods glide silently in single file between snowy pine trees, almost invisible against the snow, rifles slung on their backs.

scenes.narration: Daylight lasted only a few hours, so a patrol could strike from the gloom and be gone before anyone fired back.
scenes.caption: FEW HOURS OF LIGHT
scenes.picture: A dim blue twilight forest in deep winter. A Finnish ski soldier in a white cape and hood raises one arm to signal, while two shadowy comrades vanish into the dark trees, thin orange glow on the horizon.

scenes.narration: At night, freezing soldiers lit campfires, and the flames showed the Finns exactly where to find them.
scenes.caption: FIRES IN THE DARK
scenes.picture: Three huddled soldiers in dark brown greatcoats sit around a bright campfire in a snowy forest clearing at night, orange glow lighting their tired faces, dark trees all around them.

scenes.narration: Finnish skiers watched that glow from the dark, and crept a little closer.
scenes.caption: WATCHING
scenes.picture: Close view of a Finnish ski soldier in a white hood crouching behind a snowy spruce branch at night, his eyes lit by a distant orange glow of a campfire seen between the trees.

scenes.narration: Now back to that forest road. In early January, a whole Soviet division was stretched along it, for many kilometres.
scenes.caption: BACK TO THE ROAD
scenes.picture: A very long line of soldiers, horses, trucks and tanks stretched out along a snowy forest road that disappears into the misty distance, seen from a high snowy ridge, early January daylight.

scenes.narration: The Finns didn't try to stop it head-on. They cut it into pieces, like cutting one long rope into short ones.
scenes.caption: CUT IN PIECES
scenes.picture: A thick rope laid across fresh snow being chopped in two by a large axe held by a Finnish soldier in a white cape and hood, a snowy road with a stopped column faintly visible behind him.

scenes.narration: They called the trapped pieces 'motti', a Finnish word for a stack of firewood left in the forest.
scenes.caption: MOTTI
scenes.picture: Neat stacks of cut firewood logs piled in a snowy forest clearing beside a small wooden shed, soft snowfall, warm light on the logs, no people.

scenes.narration: Each pocket sat in the cold, cut off, unable to drag its heavy guns through deep snow.
scenes.caption: TRAPPED
scenes.picture: A small circle of exhausted Soviet soldiers in dark brown coats around a stuck cannon in deep snow in a forest clearing, surrounded by tall pines on every side, grey sky, hopeless mood.

scenes.narration: Then the Finns raided the field kitchens, because in that cold, a soldier without hot food weakens fast.
scenes.caption: NO HOT FOOD
scenes.picture: A big iron field kitchen cauldron on wheels, steam rising into the cold air, stands in a snowy forest at dusk, while one hungry soldier in a thin brown coat holds an empty metal bowl in the foreground.

scenes.narration: That explains the road. But what about the tanks? The Finns had very little to stop them.
scenes.caption: WHAT ABOUT TANKS?
scenes.picture: A huge dark green Soviet tank rumbles straight toward the camera through snowy pines, gun pointing forward, while a tiny Finnish soldier in a white cape watches from a snow bank with a worried face.

scenes.narration: So they added what they could: logs across roads, mines, satchel charges, and bottles filled with petrol.
scenes.caption: IMPROVISING
scenes.picture: Close-up of a Finnish soldier's gloved hands pushing a cloth rag into the neck of a glass bottle filled with liquid, other bottles lined up on a wooden crate beside a satchel, dim bunker light.

scenes.narration: Moscow's foreign minister, Molotov, claimed Soviet bombers were dropping food, not bombs. The Finns called the bombs 'Molotov's bread baskets.'
scenes.caption: BREAD BASKETS
scenes.picture: A wicker basket of bread loaves sits in the snow in front of a bombed wooden house with a shattered roof and smoke rising behind, a lone Finnish villager in a shawl looks on with a bitter smile.

scenes.narration: So the petrol bottles became the drink to go with the bread. The world still calls them Molotov cocktails.
scenes.caption: MOLOTOV COCKTAIL
scenes.picture: A glass bottle with a burning rag flies through the air toward a dark green Soviet tank in a snowy forest, bright orange flame trailing in the dusk, a Finnish soldier in a white cape finishing his throw.

scenes.narration: The third theory is one man: Simo Häyhä, a farmer from the Finnish countryside who became a sniper.
scenes.caption: THEORY THREE
scenes.picture: A small young Finnish farmer with a plain wool cap, round weathered face and brown work coat holds an old rifle, standing by a wooden barn in the snowy countryside, calm quiet expression.

scenes.narration: Dressed in white, he lay in the snow with a rifle, keeping snow in his mouth so his breath wouldn't show.
scenes.caption: INVISIBLE
scenes.picture: A sniper in a full white hooded suit lies flat in deep snow behind a small snow mound, only his calm face and rifle barrel visible, aiming down a quiet snowy forest, no breath cloud.

scenes.narration: Soviet soldiers called him the White Death. He's credited with 505 sniper kills, a number nobody can fully verify.
scenes.caption: THE WHITE DEATH
scenes.picture: A ghostly white-clad figure stands among snowy pine trees in thick mist, barely visible, while two nervous Soviet soldiers in dark brown coats crouch in the foreground, staring at him in fear.

scenes.narration: In March 1940, a bullet tore through his jaw. He survived, and woke up on the day the war ended.
scenes.caption: MARCH 1940
scenes.picture: A young Finnish soldier with a bandaged jaw and wrapped face lies in a narrow cot in a plain wooden hospital ward, a nurse in a white apron and cap stands beside him, soft window light.

scenes.narration: But one sniper can't stop an army. Finland's whole stand spread courage and made the world watch. Häyhä became the symbol later.
scenes.caption: A SYMBOL
scenes.picture: Three ordinary Finnish people in 1930s coats sit around a wooden radio on a kitchen table, listening with hopeful faces, soft lamp light, a steaming kettle on the stove behind them.

scenes.narration: By February, though, the Finns were in trouble. Men were exhausted, and shells were running low.
scenes.caption: FEBRUARY 1940
scenes.picture: Exhausted Finnish soldiers with frost-covered faces and sunken eyes sit slumped in a muddy snowy trench, one holding an almost empty wooden ammunition box, grey dawn light.

scenes.narration: The Soviets had learned from their mistakes. They brought fresh troops, new tactics and an enormous amount of artillery.
scenes.caption: THE SOVIETS ADAPT
scenes.picture: A long row of big artillery guns lined up on a snowy field, Soviet soldiers in brown winter coats loading shells, dark smoke on the horizon, cold grey sky.

scenes.narration: Near Summa, on the Karelian Isthmus, shells hammered the Finnish trenches day and night.
scenes.caption: SUMMA
scenes.picture: A snowy battlefield with exploding shells throwing plumes of black earth and snow around a log-covered Finnish trench, one soldier in a white cape covering his head, smoke across the sky.

scenes.narration: In mid-February the line finally cracked, and Finnish troops fell back toward Viipuri, one of their biggest cities.
scenes.caption: THE LINE CRACKS
scenes.picture: A tired column of Finnish soldiers in white capes retreats on skis and on foot across a snowy plain toward a distant town with church towers, smoke rising behind them.

scenes.narration: Mannerheim warned his government that the army couldn't hold much longer. Finland had to choose.
scenes.caption: A HARD CHOICE
scenes.picture: An elderly tall Finnish general with white hair, stern lined face and a long grey military greatcoat stands before two anxious men in dark suits around a table in a plain government room, lamp light, serious faces.

scenes.narration: Keep fighting and risk losing everything, or stop and lose something. They chose to stop.
scenes.caption: FIGHT OR STOP
scenes.picture: A man in a dark overcoat holds a pen above a single sheet of paper on a wooden desk, hesitating with a heavy troubled face, a snowy window behind him, dim lamp light.

scenes.narration: On 13 March 1940, after one hundred and five days, the guns fell silent.
scenes.caption: 13 MARCH 1940
scenes.picture: A quiet snowy forest at dawn, smoke curling up from a lone abandoned trench, a Finnish ski soldier in a white cape lowers his rifle and looks up at the pale sky, stillness.

scenes.narration: The price was heavy. Finland gave up about a tenth of its land, including Viipuri and most of the Karelian Isthmus.
scenes.caption: LAND LOST
scenes.picture: A Finnish family stands at a wooden gate looking back at their farmhouse and snowy fields, the mother wiping her eyes, a sled loaded with bundles beside them, grey cold light.

scenes.narration: About four hundred thousand people left their homes, loading sleds and carts with whatever they could carry.
scenes.caption: 400,000 LEAVE
scenes.picture: A long line of horse-drawn carts and sleds loaded with furniture, bedding and bundled children winds along a snowy country road, tired adults in coats walking beside the horses.

scenes.narration: Roughly twenty-five thousand Finnish soldiers had died. Soviet records later admitted well over a hundred thousand dead or missing.
scenes.caption: THE COST
scenes.picture: Rows of simple wooden crosses in a snowy forest cemetery, small candles glowing in glass jars on the snow, dusk blue light, a lone old woman in a dark shawl kneeling among them.

scenes.narration: But look at what didn't change. Finland kept its government, its army and its flag. It stayed independent.
scenes.caption: STILL INDEPENDENT
scenes.picture: A Finnish town square in early spring, ordinary people in coats walking across wet cobbles with melting snow, a plain blue-and-white flag waving on a tall pole against a clearing sky.

scenes.narration: So how did Finland hold on? Not a wall, not the weather, and not one sniper.
scenes.caption: THE ANSWER
scenes.picture: A huge dark shadow of a giant looms over a small snowy forest village at dusk, while small cottage windows glow warm and defiant, dramatic storybook mood, no people.

scenes.narration: It was a country that knew its forest like a backyard, and fought on ground the invaders couldn't use.
scenes.caption: KNOWING THE LAND
scenes.picture: A broad sweeping view of a vast frozen lake surrounded by dense snowy pine forest in low golden light, a tiny line of Finnish ski soldiers in white capes crossing the ice.

scenes.narration: Soviet troops were tied to roads. Finnish skiers moved between them, where tanks couldn't follow.
scenes.caption: ROADS VS SKIS
scenes.picture: A Finnish ski patrol in white capes glides fast through deep snow between tall pines, far from any road, while far behind them a stuck line of tanks sits on a narrow snowy road.

scenes.narration: And every kilometre they gave up cost the attackers dearly, which bought time to keep the country alive.
scenes.caption: BUYING TIME
scenes.picture: A small Finnish ski soldier in a long white cape and grey wool cap, asleep on a wooden bunk in a snowy forest cabin, his skis leaning on the wall, a glowing iron stove and a cup of hot tea beside him.

scenes.narration: And the border near Leningrad? It did move away from the city, much further than Moscow first asked. Finland paid in land.
scenes.caption: BORDER MOVED
scenes.picture: Two men in dark overcoats hammer a plain wooden border post into frozen ground on a wide snowy plain, a faint city skyline far away on the horizon, cold pale light.

scenes.narration: Finland lost the war but kept its independence, thanks to terrain, tactics and Soviet mistakes, not a single wonder weapon.
scenes.caption: LAND FOR FREEDOM
scenes.picture: A Finnish farmer and his wife stand together in front of a small new wooden cabin in a snowy clearing, hands on each other's shoulders, smoke rising from the chimney, a hopeful faint sunrise.

scenes.narration: Today, rows of granite tank blocks still stand in the woods of the Karelian Isthmus.
scenes.caption: STILL STANDING
scenes.picture: A modern-day quiet pine forest in summer light, long rows of weathered grey granite tank blocks half covered in moss, green ferns around them, no people, peaceful.

scenes.narration: On that silent road, the Finns gathered up the abandoned guns and tanks to re-arm. Finland lost the war, but that winter belonged to the people who knew the woods.
scenes.delivery: warm, closing the loop, slow finish
scenes.caption: THE QUIET ROAD
scenes.picture: Three Finnish soldiers in white capes haul a captured Soviet field gun with ropes along a narrow snowy forest road at dusk, abandoned tanks and trucks beside them, soft blue light.

narrator: Gripping investigative storyteller, low and intense, leaning in, building suspense, quick between clues.

short.title: How Tiny Finland Survived the Soviet Union
short.description:
In 1939 the huge Soviet Union invaded tiny Finland. How did Finland hold on for 105 days? The Winter War in under a minute.
Sources: Finnish Defence Forces history of the Winter War; Britannica, "Winter War".

scenes.narration: In 1939, the huge Soviet Union invaded tiny Finland, so how did Finland survive?
scenes.caption: FINLAND, 1939
scenes.picture: Finnish ski soldier, young man with a white hooded cape and grey wool cap, wide frightened eyes, face big and central, looking down a snowy forest road where a long line of Soviet tanks and trucks waits far behind, pale winter light, Finland 1939

scenes.narration: Finland had under four million people; the Soviets, one hundred seventy million.
scenes.delivery: slow, letting the gap sink in
scenes.caption: 3.7M vs 170M
scenes.picture: Four Finnish farmers in dark wool coats and fur caps standing close together in the snow in the foreground, small and nervous, facing a vast dark mass of Soviet soldiers in brown greatcoats blurred along the whole horizon, grey winter sky, Finland 1939

scenes.narration: Soviet leaders wanted Finland's border moved, since it sat thirty-two kilometres from Leningrad.
scenes.caption: 32 KM AWAY
scenes.picture: Large old field cannon with a dark iron barrel in the foreground, pointing across a flat autumn plain of bare birch and pine trees toward a faint city skyline with one golden spire on the hazy horizon, cold light, Leningrad 1939

scenes.narration: Finland refused, so on 30 November 1939, Soviet troops invaded.
scenes.caption: 30 NOV 1939
scenes.picture: Two worried Finnish civilians, a middle-aged man in a dark wool coat and fur cap and a woman in a headscarf and long coat, looking up at the pale sky, black smoke rising over Helsinki rooftops behind them, 30 November 1939

scenes.narration: Soviet columns stuck to narrow roads, but Finnish skiers in white capes glided through forests.
scenes.caption: WHITE CAPES
scenes.picture: Three Finnish ski soldiers in long white hooded capes gliding in single file between snowy pine trees, almost invisible against the snow, a narrow forest road with a stalled line of Soviet tanks seen beside them, Finland winter 1939

scenes.narration: So the Finns cut those columns into pieces and trapped freezing soldiers.
scenes.caption: TRAPPED
scenes.picture: Group of exhausted Soviet soldiers in thin dark brown greatcoats and fur-less caps huddled around a stuck field cannon in deep snow, frost on their faces, tall dark pines around them, hopeless mood, Finland winter 1940

scenes.narration: But by February 1940, Finland's army was running out of shells.
scenes.caption: FEBRUARY 1940
scenes.picture: Tired Finnish soldier, young man in a white hooded cape with a frost-covered face and sunken eyes, slumped in a muddy snowy trench, holding an almost empty wooden ammunition box open in his hands, grey dawn light, February 1940

scenes.narration: Soviet guns cracked the line, so Finland's Marshal Mannerheim warned the army couldn't hold.
scenes.caption: MANNERHEIM
scenes.picture: Marshal Mannerheim, elderly Finnish general with short white hair and a stern weary face, long grey military greatcoat, standing in a plain wood-panelled government room before two anxious men in dark suits, warm lamp light, 1940

scenes.narration: On 13 March 1940, after 105 days, the guns fell silent.
scenes.caption: 13 MARCH 1940
scenes.picture: Finnish soldier in a white hooded cape lowering his rifle and gazing up at a pale dawn sky, calm exhausted face big and central, thin smoke curling from an abandoned snowy trench behind him in a quiet pine forest, 13 March 1940

scenes.narration: Finland lost land, but it stayed independent.
scenes.caption: STILL FREE
scenes.picture: Finnish family at a wooden farm gate looking back at their snowy red wooden farmhouse, the mother in a headscarf wiping her eyes, father in a wool coat and fur cap beside a sled loaded with bundles, grey cold light, Finland 1940

scenes.narration: So Finland survived because its skiers fought in forests tanks couldn't enter.
scenes.caption: THE ANSWER
scenes.picture: Finnish ski patrol of two soldiers in white hooded capes gliding fast between tall snowy pines, big in the foreground, a lone stuck Soviet tank on a narrow snowy road far behind them, golden low winter sun, Finland 1940
